questions.stem: The nurse is assisting a client with left-sided weakness to transfer from the bed to a chair. Where should the nurse position the chair?

options.text: On the client's left (weak) side so the client pivots toward the weaker side.
On the client's right (strong) side so the client can use the stronger side to pivot.
Directly at the foot of the bed so the client does not need to turn.
In front of the bed so the client can move straight forward.

rationales.whyCorrect: During a transfer, the chair should be positioned on the client's strong side so the client can use their stronger arm and leg to pivot and assist with the transfer. This reduces the risk of falls and injury to both the client and the nurse. Positioning on the weak side (A) prevents the client from using their strength. Transferring straight forward (C, D) requires more strength and control.
rationales.eli10:
- The client is weak on the left side. Put the chair on the strong right side.

- The client uses the strong arm and leg to push up and turn toward the chair.

- Always let the client use their strong side. It is safer.

- Chair on the strong side = less chance of falling.

questions.stem: The nurse is repositioning a client who is immobile. Which position change is most effective for preventing a pressure injury over the sacrum?

options.text: Repositioning the client from side to side every 4 hours.
Repositioning the client at least every 2 hours using a draw sheet.
Keeping the client in a supine position with the head of the bed elevated to 60 degrees.
Placing a donut-shaped cushion under the client's sacrum for pressure relief.

rationales.whyCorrect: Repositioning immobile clients at least every 2 hours using a draw sheet reduces sustained pressure on bony prominences and prevents pressure injuries. A donut-shaped cushion (D) actually increases pressure around the edges and can worsen tissue ischemia. Positioning in supine at 60 degrees (C) increases sacral pressure from shearing. Repositioning every 4 hours (A) is too infrequent.
rationales.eli10:
- The client cannot move on their own. Every 2 hours, the nurse uses a sheet to gently turn the client to a new position.

- This keeps pressure off one spot too long. Pressure that stays in one place too long cuts off blood flow and makes a sore.

- A donut pillow sounds helpful but actually squeezes the skin worse.

- Turn every 2 hours. Use a draw sheet to slide, not drag.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to feed a client with dysphagia. Which action should the nurse take to reduce the risk of aspiration?

options.text: Position the client in a supine position with the head flat.
Encourage the client to drink thin liquids quickly to minimize mouth pooling.
Position the client upright at a 90-degree angle and instruct them to tuck the chin before swallowing.
Offer the client a straw to help control the flow of liquids.

rationales.whyCorrect: For a client with dysphagia, the safest position is sitting upright at 90 degrees with the chin tucked before swallowing. Chin tucking closes the airway and directs food toward the esophagus. A supine position (A) greatly increases aspiration risk. Thin liquids (B) are the most difficult to swallow safely. A straw (D) delivers fluid rapidly to the back of the throat, increasing aspiration risk.
rationales.eli10:
- The client has trouble swallowing. Sit them straight up.

- Before they swallow, tell them to put their chin down toward their chest. This closes the breathing tube so food goes to the stomach, not the lungs.

- No straws. No thin, watery drinks. Thick drinks are easier to control.

- Sit up, chin down, small bites.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing perineal care to a female client. Which direction should the nurse use when cleansing the perineal area?

options.text: From the anal area toward the pubic area (back to front).
From the pubic area toward the anal area (front to back).
In a circular motion starting at the anal area.
The direction does not matter if a clean washcloth is used for each stroke.

rationales.whyCorrect: Perineal care should be performed from front to back (pubic area toward anal area) to prevent introducing fecal organisms into the urethra, which could cause a urinary tract infection. Back to front (A) would spread fecal bacteria toward the urethra. Circular motions starting at the anus (C) also risk contamination. Direction always matters (D).
rationales.eli10:
- When cleaning the private area, always wipe from front to back.

- This keeps stool germs away from the pee opening (urethra) so they do not cause an infection.

- Wipe once, use a clean part of the cloth, then wipe again. Never go back to front.

- Front to back, every time.

questions.stem: A client with an indwelling urinary catheter is being assisted with bathing by a UAP. Which action by the UAP requires intervention by the nurse?

options.text: The UAP wears clean gloves during perineal care.
The UAP keeps the drainage bag below the level of the client's bladder.
The UAP cleanses the catheter tubing by wiping from the meatus outward.
The UAP tapes the catheter to the client's inner thigh for secure placement.

rationales.whyCorrect: Taping the catheter to the inner thigh should be done by attaching it to the upper thigh (for female clients) or lower abdomen (for males), not the inner thigh where tension and movement can cause urethral trauma. The inner thigh is not the standard securement site. Wearing clean gloves (A), keeping the bag below the bladder (B), and cleaning from meatus outward (C) are all correct.
rationales.eli10:
- A catheter (pee tube) must be taped in the right place. For women, it goes on the upper thigh. For men, on the lower belly.

- Taping it to the inner thigh can pull on the tube and hurt the inside of the body.

- The UAP should be stopped and shown the right place.

- The bag must always hang lower than the bladder.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a stage 2 pressure injury on the heel. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Massage the area around the pressure injury to promote circulation.
Apply a protective dressing and relieve pressure by floating the heel off the bed surface.
Clean the wound with hydrogen peroxide and pack it with sterile gauze.
Apply a heating pad to the site to increase blood flow and promote healing.

rationales.whyCorrect: A stage 2 pressure injury involves partial-thickness skin loss. Treatment includes protecting the wound with an appropriate dressing and completely relieving pressure from the area — floating the heel off the bed using pillows or a heel-suspension device. Massaging a pressure injury (A) causes further tissue damage. Hydrogen peroxide (C) is cytotoxic to healing tissue. Heat (D) increases metabolic demand and can worsen ischemia.
rationales.eli10:
- The heel has a skin sore. The nurse covers it with a special dressing and floats the heel so nothing touches the bed.

- Massaging a sore makes it worse. It damages the tissue more.

- Do not use strong cleaners like hydrogen peroxide. They hurt healing skin.

- Float the heel. No pressure at all.

questions.stem: A client who is on bed rest has not had a bowel movement in 4 days. The client reports feeling bloated. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Administer the prescribed PRN laxative.
Insert a rectal suppository as ordered.
Assess the client's abdomen, bowel sounds, and usual bowel pattern.
Increase the client's IV fluid rate to stimulate peristalsis.

rationales.whyCorrect: Before administering any intervention for constipation, the nurse must first assess the client's abdomen (distention, tenderness), bowel sounds (presence, quality), and usual bowel pattern. This helps determine the appropriate intervention. Administering a laxative (A) or suppository (B) before assessment could be inappropriate. The nurse cannot independently increase IV fluids (D).
rationales.eli10:
- The client has not pooped in 4 days and feels bloated. The nurse checks the belly first.

- The nurse listens for bowel sounds with a stethoscope and gently presses on the belly to see if it is hard or painful.

- After checking, the nurse decides what to do. Maybe a laxative is ordered. Maybe something else is needed.

- Assess first. Then act.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about the use of a cane. The client has weakness in the right leg. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?

options.text: "I will hold the cane in my right hand."
"I will hold the cane in my left hand and move it forward with my right leg."
"I will hold the cane in my left hand and move it forward with my left leg."
"I will use the cane only when I am walking outside my home."

rationales.whyCorrect: A cane is held on the strong side (opposite the weak leg) to provide the widest base of support. The cane is advanced forward simultaneously with the weak leg, then the strong leg follows. Holding the cane on the weak side (A) does not provide proper support. Moving the cane with the strong leg (C) is incorrect.
rationales.eli10:
- The right leg is weak. Hold the cane in the left hand (the strong side).

- Move the cane forward at the same time as the weak right leg. Then the strong left leg steps up.

- The cane acts like a third leg on the strong side to help balance the weak side.

- Cane in the strong hand. Cane and weak leg move together.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who is receiving continuous enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube. Which action is most important for preventing aspiration?

options.text: Keeping the head of the bed elevated at least 30 to 45 degrees during the feeding.
Checking gastric residual volume every 12 hours.
Using a small-bore feeding tube to reduce reflux.
Flushing the tube with 30 mL of water every 2 hours.

rationales.whyCorrect: Keeping the head of the bed elevated at least 30 to 45 degrees during continuous tube feeding significantly reduces the risk of aspiration by using gravity to keep stomach contents down. Checking residual volume every 12 hours (B) is too infrequent — it is typically checked every 4 to 6 hours. Tube size alone (C) does not prevent aspiration.
rationales.eli10:
- Tube feeding goes into the stomach. The head of the bed must be up at least 30 to 45 degrees.

- Gravity keeps the liquid food in the stomach. If the client lies flat, the food can come back up and go into the lungs.

- Head up = food stays down. Head flat = risk of choking on stomach contents.

- Always check the head of the bed before starting or continuing a tube feeding.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing oral care to an unconscious client. What is the safest position for the client during oral care?

options.text: Supine with the head turned to one side toward the nurse.
Flat with the chin extended upward.
Side-lying with the head turned toward the basin.
Semi-Fowler's position with the neck hyperextended.

rationales.whyCorrect: The side-lying position with the head turned toward the basin allows fluids to drain out of the mouth by gravity, reducing the risk of aspiration during oral care. Supine (A) allows fluid to pool in the back of the throat. Neck hyperextension (D) increases aspiration risk. Semi-Fowler's position (D) may be used if the client has an artificial airway with a cuff inflated.
rationales.eli10:
- The client is unconscious and cannot swallow or cough on purpose.

- Turn the client on their side with the head tilted so any liquid runs out of the mouth into a basin, not down the throat.

- This stops the client from choking on mouth rinse.

- Gravity is your friend. Let the liquid drain out.

questions.stem: A client has been on bed rest for 5 days and is now being assisted to sit on the edge of the bed for the first time. The client suddenly reports feeling lightheaded and dizzy. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Help the client lie back down and monitor vital signs.
Tell the client to take deep, slow breaths while remaining seated.
Encourage the client to stand quickly to overcome the dizziness.
Continue with the activity because dizziness is expected with initial mobilization.

rationales.whyCorrect: Lightheadedness and dizziness when first sitting up after prolonged bed rest suggest orthostatic hypotension. The nurse should help the client lie back down immediately to prevent a fall and monitor vital signs (lying, sitting, and standing as tolerated). Deep breaths (B) will not resolve orthostatic hypotension. Standing quickly (C) could cause syncope and injury. Dizziness should never be ignored (D).
rationales.eli10:
- The client has been in bed for 5 days. Sitting up makes them dizzy.

- This is because blood pressure drops when the body changes position too fast after lying down for days.

- Help the client lie back down right away so they do not fall.

- Check blood pressure. Go slower next time. Sit up in stages.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client's skin and notes a reddened area over the coccyx that does not blanch when pressed with a fingertip. How should the nurse stage this pressure injury?

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury.
Stage 2 pressure injury.
Deep tissue pressure injury.
Unstageable pressure injury.

rationales.whyCorrect: A stage 1 pressure injury presents as intact skin with non-blanchable erythema (redness that does not blanch/turn white when pressed). The skin is not broken. Stage 2 (B) involves partial-thickness skin loss. Deep tissue injury (C) presents as a purple or maroon area of intact skin or a blood-filled blister. Unstageable (D) involves full-thickness tissue loss covered by slough or eschar.
rationales.eli10:
- The skin is red, but when pressed, the red stays. It does not turn white. This is a stage 1 pressure sore.

- The skin is not broken yet. The damage is underneath.

- If pressure is removed now, this can heal. If pressure stays, it gets worse.

- Stage 1 = red that stays red when pressed.

questions.stem: The nurse is assisting a client with range-of-motion exercises. The client has contractures of the right elbow. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Forcefully stretch the elbow to break the contracture.
Perform passive range of motion up to the point of resistance without forcing the joint.
Avoid moving the right arm entirely to prevent pain.
Apply heat to the elbow for 30 minutes before attempting full range of motion.

rationales.whyCorrect: For a client with contractures, passive range of motion should be performed gently up to the point of resistance. Forcing the joint (A) can cause fractures, pain, and soft tissue injury. Avoiding movement (C) would worsen the contracture. Heat (D) may be used but should not be applied before forcing the joint beyond its limit.
rationales.eli10:
- The client's elbow is stiff and cannot straighten all the way. The nurse moves it gently only as far as it goes easily.

- If the nurse pushes harder, the bone or tissue could tear.

- Do not force a stiff joint. Move it only to the point where it naturally stops.

- Gentle, slow, no forcing.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about collecting a clean-catch (midstream) urine specimen. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: "Collect the first stream of urine in the cup."
"Clean the perineal area, then urinate a small amount into the toilet before collecting the specimen."
"Collect the specimen immediately after a shower without cleaning the area."
"Fill the specimen cup to the very top with urine."

rationales.whyCorrect: A clean-catch urine specimen requires cleaning the perineal area, then starting to urinate to flush the urethra, and collecting the midstream portion in the sterile cup. The first stream (A) contains urethral contaminants. Collecting after a shower without cleaning (C) may still have contaminants. Overfilling the cup (D) may cause spillage and contamination.
rationales.eli10:
- The client cleans the private area with a special wipe.

- Then they start to pee in the toilet first (this washes out the opening).

- Then they catch the middle part of the pee stream in the cup.

- Do not catch the very first or very last drops. The middle is cleanest.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a fiberglass cast on the lower leg that was applied 1 hour ago. Which action is the nurse's priority during the first 24 hours?

options.text: Perform neurovascular checks on the affected extremity every hour.
Cover the cast with a plastic bag to keep it clean.
Elevate the leg only when the client is in bed.
Instruct the client to insert a coat hanger into the cast to scratch any itching.

rationales.whyCorrect: During the first 24 hours after cast application, the priority is monitoring neurovascular status (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and temperature) hourly to detect compartment syndrome. Covering the cast (B) is about cleanliness, not the priority. Elevation (C) should be maintained above the heart level continuously for the first 24 to 48 hours, not only when in bed. A coat hanger (D) should never be inserted into a cast because it can break the skin and introduce infection.
rationales.eli10:
- A new cast means the leg might swell inside. If it swells too much, blood flow is cut off — that is dangerous.

- The nurse checks every hour: can the client feel touch? Wiggle toes? Are toes pink and warm? Does it hurt a lot?

- Never put anything inside the cast to scratch. It can cut the skin and cause a bad infection.

- The cast must stay dry and clean.

questions.stem: A client is receiving intermittent enteral tube feedings. The nurse checks the gastric residual volume before the next feeding and obtains 180 mL. The prescription states to hold the feeding if residual is greater than 150 mL. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Administer the feeding because 180 mL is close to the limit.
Hold the feeding, return the residual, and notify the healthcare provider.
Discard the residual, flush the tube, and administer the feeding.
Dilute the residual with water and administer it with the next feeding.

rationales.whyCorrect: The gastric residual volume of 180 mL exceeds the ordered hold parameter of 150 mL. The nurse should hold the feeding, return the residual (to prevent electrolyte imbalances from discarding digestive fluids), and notify the provider. Administering despite exceeding the limit (A) risks aspiration. Discarding (C) wastes digestive enzymes and electrolytes. Diluting (D) does not address the delayed gastric emptying.
rationales.eli10:
- There is too much leftover food in the stomach (180 mL, and the limit is 150).

- The stomach is not emptying properly. Pushing more food in could make the client vomit and choke.

- The nurse stops the feeding, puts the leftover back (it has important stuff the body needs), and calls the provider.

- High leftover = hold the feeding.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about measures to prevent constipation. Which statement by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I should avoid drinking water with my meals to prevent bloating."
"I should increase my intake of high-fiber foods and drink plenty of fluids every day."
"I should take a laxative every day to keep my bowels regular."
"I should hold my bowel movements as long as possible to build up pressure."

rationales.whyCorrect: A high-fiber diet (fruits, vegetables, whole grains) combined with adequate fluid intake promotes regular bowel movements and prevents constipation. Avoiding water (A) worsens constipation. Daily laxatives (C) can cause dependence and electrolyte imbalances. Holding bowel movements (D) leads to harder stools and worsening constipation.
rationales.eli10:
- Eating lots of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains (fiber) plus drinking plenty of water keeps poop soft and moving.

- Fiber without water is like a dry sponge — it gets stuck. Fiber plus water works well.

- Do not take laxatives every day. The body can forget how to poop on its own.

- Go when you feel the urge. Holding it makes it harder.

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a client's understanding of crutch walking using a three-point gait after a below-knee amputation. Which observation indicates correct technique?

options.text: The client moves both crutches and the affected leg forward together, then moves the unaffected leg.
The client moves the right crutch, then the left foot, then the left crutch, then the right foot.
The client swings both feet forward at the same time past the crutches.
The client moves the unaffected leg forward first, followed by the crutches.

rationales.whyCorrect: The three-point gait is used when one leg cannot bear weight (such as after an amputation). Both crutches and the affected (or missing) leg move forward together, then the unaffected leg swings through. Options B (four-point gait) and C (swing-through gait) describe different crutch-walking patterns.
rationales.eli10:
- The client has one leg. They use two crutches plus their one good leg — that makes three points.

- Move both crutches and the "empty" leg spot forward together. Then hop the good leg up.

- This is the three-point gait.

- Crutches and the bad side move together. Good leg follows.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client who has been receiving IV fluids for 3 days. The nurse notes that the client has crackles in the lung bases, 2+ pitting edema in the lower extremities, and an intake that exceeds output by 1,200 mL over the past 24 hours. What condition do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Dehydration.
Fluid-volume overload.
Hypokalemia.
Respiratory acidosis.

rationales.whyCorrect: Crackles in the lungs, peripheral edema, and intake significantly exceeding output are classic signs of fluid-volume overload (hypervolemia). The heart and kidneys are unable to handle the excess fluid. Dehydration (A) would present with dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, and low urine output. Hypokalemia (C) presents with muscle weakness and cardiac changes. Respiratory acidosis (D) is related to CO2 retention.
rationales.eli10:
- Too much fluid is in the body. The lungs are getting wet (crackles), the legs are puffy (edema), and more fluid went in than came out.

- The body cannot get rid of the extra fluid fast enough.

- This can strain the heart and make breathing hard.

- Dehydration is not enough fluid — this is the opposite.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who requires a 24-hour urine collection. The collection begins at 0800. At 0800, the client voids 200 mL. What should the nurse do with this specimen?

options.text: Add it to the 24-hour collection container.
Discard it and begin collecting all subsequent urine for the next 24 hours.
Send it to the laboratory as a separate specimen.
Measure it and document it but do not add it to the collection.

rationales.whyCorrect: For a 24-hour urine collection, the first voided specimen at the start time is discarded, and all subsequent urine for the next 24 hours is collected. Adding the first void (A) would include urine produced before the collection period began, invalidating the results.
rationales.eli10:
- The collection starts at 8 AM. The client pees at 8 AM. Throw that pee away.

- Then save EVERY drop of pee for the next 24 hours, until 8 AM the next day.

- The first one does not count because it was made before the test started.

- Discard the first one. Save all the rest.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer an enema to an adult client. In which position should the nurse place the client?

options.text: Supine with the legs extended.
Left lateral (Sims') position with the right knee flexed.
Right lateral position with the left knee flexed.
Prone with the head turned to one side.

rationales.whyCorrect: The left lateral (Sims') position with the right knee flexed allows the enema solution to flow by gravity along the natural curve of the sigmoid colon, promoting retention and effectiveness. The supine position (A) works against gravity. Right lateral (C) is less effective for reaching the sigmoid colon.
rationales.eli10:
- The enema goes into the bottom. The client lies on the left side with the top knee bent up.

- This position lets the fluid flow into the colon naturally, following the curve of the bowel.

- Left side down. Right knee up. Gravity helps.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing hygiene care to an older adult client. Which consideration is most important when caring for the older adult's skin?

options.text: Bathe the client daily with hot water and a deodorant soap to prevent odor.
Use lukewarm water, mild soap, and apply moisturizer to prevent dryness and skin breakdown.
Apply lotion only to the client's hands and face, avoiding the legs.
Rub the skin vigorously with a towel after bathing to stimulate circulation.

rationales.whyCorrect: Older adult skin is thinner, drier, and more fragile. Use lukewarm water (not hot), mild soap, and apply moisturizer to prevent dryness and skin breakdown. Hot water (A) strips natural oils. Lotion should be applied to all skin, not just hands and face (C). Vigorous rubbing (D) can damage fragile skin.
rationales.eli10:
- Older skin is thin and dry like tissue paper.

- Use warm (not hot) water, gentle soap, and lotion all over.

- Pat the skin dry — do not rub hard.

- Hot water and hard rubbing damage older skin.

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for "0.9% sodium chloride IV at 100 mL/hr." The client currently has an IV of 0.9% sodium chloride infusing at 75 mL/hr with approximately 250 mL remaining in the bag. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Continue the current rate until the bag is empty, then start the new rate.
Adjust the infusion rate to 100 mL/hr.
Call the provider to clarify whether the current bag can be used at the new rate.
Discontinue the current IV and start a new one at the correct rate.

rationales.whyCorrect: The new prescription is for the same fluid at a higher rate. The nurse should adjust the infusion rate to the new ordered rate of 100 mL/hr. There is no need to wait for the current bag to finish (A) or start a new IV (D) because the fluid is the same solution. Calling the provider (C) is unnecessary for a simple rate adjustment on the same fluid.
rationales.eli10:
- The fluid is the same (normal saline). The order just changes how fast it goes in.

- The nurse changes the pump from 75 to 100 mL/hr.

- No need to call the doctor or start a new IV. It is the same fluid, just faster.

- Adjust the rate. That is all.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a UAP about providing foot care to a client with diabetes mellitus. Which statement by the UAP indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I should wash the client's feet with warm water and mild soap."
"I should dry the feet thoroughly, especially between the toes."
"I should apply lotion between the client's toes to prevent cracking."
"I should inspect the client's feet and report any cuts or red areas to the nurse."

rationales.whyCorrect: Lotion should NOT be applied between the toes because moisture trapped between the toes can promote fungal growth and skin breakdown. Washing with warm water and mild soap (A), drying thoroughly (B), and inspecting and reporting abnormalities (D) are all correct foot-care practices for a client with diabetes.
rationales.eli10:
- The UAP should put lotion on the feet but NOT between the toes.

- Moisture trapped between toes can grow fungus and cause infections.

- Dry between the toes well. Lotion on top and bottom of feet, but skip between the toes.

- Diabetic feet need extra care because small injuries can become big problems.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer an intramuscular injection to an adult client. Which site is most appropriate for a volume of 3 mL?

options.text: Deltoid muscle.
Ventrogluteal site.
Vastus lateralis muscle.
Dorsogluteal site.

rationales.whyCorrect: The ventrogluteal site can safely accommodate up to 3 mL of medication in an adult and is the preferred site for larger volumes due to its large muscle mass and fewer major blood vessels and nerves. The deltoid (A) holds a maximum of about 1 mL. The vastus lateralis (C) can hold up to 2–3 mL but the ventrogluteal is preferred. The dorsogluteal (D) is no longer recommended due to proximity to the sciatic nerve.
rationales.eli10:
- For a big injection (3 mL), the nurse uses the hip muscle (ventrogluteal site).

- The arm muscle (deltoid) can only hold 1 mL.

- The hip muscle is big, has fewer big nerves and blood vessels, and is the safest choice for larger shots.

- Big shot = hip muscle.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has been immobile for several days. The client is now exhibiting calf tenderness, unilateral leg swelling, and warmth in the right lower extremity. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Massage the affected calf to promote circulation.
Apply a warm compress and elevate the leg above the heart.
Notify the healthcare provider and avoid manipulating the affected extremity.
Encourage the client to ambulate to the bathroom to improve venous return.

rationales.whyCorrect: Calf tenderness, unilateral swelling, and warmth are signs of a possible deep-vein thrombosis (DVT). The nurse must NOT massage or manipulate the leg because this could dislodge the clot, causing a pulmonary embolism. The nurse should keep the client on bed rest, elevate the leg, and notify the provider immediately. Massage (A) is dangerous. Ambulation (D) could dislodge the clot.
rationales.eli10:
- The client has a painful, swollen, warm calf after being in bed for days. This could be a blood clot in the leg.

- Never rub it. Rubbing could break the clot loose and send it to the lungs — that can kill.

- Keep the leg still and elevated. Tell the provider right away.

- Do not touch, rub, or walk on a possible blood clot.

questions.stem: A client is receiving continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) after a prostate surgery. The nurse notes that the urinary output is bright red with large clots. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document the finding and continue to monitor.
Increase the irrigation flow rate as ordered and notify the healthcare provider.
Stop the irrigation immediately and clamp the catheter.
Irrigate the catheter manually with a syringe to break up the clots.

rationales.whyCorrect: Bright red blood with large clots in the CBI output suggests active bleeding after prostate surgery. The nurse should increase the irrigation rate as ordered to clear the clots and notify the provider. Stopping the irrigation (C) could allow clots to obstruct the catheter and cause bladder distention. Manual irrigation (D) may be needed but only with a provider order.
rationales.eli10:
- After prostate surgery, fluid is run through the bladder to wash out blood.

- Bright red blood with big clots means active bleeding.

- The nurse turns up the irrigation fluid (as the order allows) to wash out the clots and calls the provider.

- Do not stop the flow. It needs to keep washing.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client how to use a walker. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: "Stand inside the walker with your back touching the back bar."
"Move the walker forward first, then step into the walker with your weaker leg first."
"Push the walker far ahead of you and take long strides to catch up."
"Pick up the walker and carry it forward with each step."

rationales.whyCorrect: Correct walker use involves moving the walker forward first, then stepping the weaker leg into the walker, followed by the stronger leg. The client should stand between the back legs of the walker, not touch the back bar (A). Pushing the walker far ahead (C) creates instability. The walker should not be lifted with each step (D) unless it is a wheeled walker.
rationales.eli10:
- Pick up the walker. Set it a small step ahead.

- Step into the walker with the weak leg first, then the strong leg.

- Do not push the walker way out in front — that is unstable.

- Small steps. Walker first, weak leg first, strong leg follows.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing care to a client who has a prescription for a clear liquid diet. Which item should the nurse offer?

options.text: Chicken broth, apple juice, and a plain gelatin dessert.
Cream of tomato soup, milk, and orange juice with pulp.
Vanilla pudding, coffee with cream, and a banana popsicle.
Oatmeal, herbal tea, and a fruit smoothie.

rationales.whyCorrect: A clear liquid diet includes fluids that are transparent and leave no residue, such as broth (without solids), clear juices without pulp, plain gelatin, tea, and black coffee. Cream soups (B), milk, pudding (C), and oatmeal (D) are not clear liquids.
rationales.eli10:
- Clear liquid means you can see through it — like water, apple juice, plain Jell-O, and broth.

- Nothing creamy. Nothing with pulp. Nothing solid.

- Milk, pudding, and oatmeal are not clear. They leave stuff in the stomach.

- See-through liquids only.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has urinary incontinence. Which intervention is most important for maintaining skin integrity?

options.text: Limit the client's fluid intake to decrease urine production.
Apply a thick layer of talcum powder to the perineal area to absorb moisture.
Cleanse the skin promptly after incontinence episodes and apply a moisture-barrier cream.
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to keep the skin dry.

rationales.whyCorrect: Prompt cleansing after incontinence episodes removes moisture and irritants (urine, stool) from the skin, and applying a moisture-barrier cream protects the skin from future exposure. Limiting fluids (A) can cause dehydration and concentrated urine that is more irritating. Talcum powder (B) can cake and cause friction. An indwelling catheter (D) is an invasive last resort with infection risks.
rationales.eli10:
- Urine and stool sitting on the skin break it down fast.

- Clean the skin right away after any accident.

- Put on a protective cream that blocks moisture (barrier cream).

- Do not use powder. Do not put in a catheter unless there is no other way.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer a medication through a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube. The nurse checks the gastric residual volume and obtains 75 mL. The prescription states to hold the feeding if the residual is greater than 100 mL. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the medication because the residual volume is elevated.
Return the residual, flush the tube, administer the medication, and resume the feeding.
Discard the residual and administer the medication with 30 mL of water.
Administer the medication but hold the feeding for 4 hours.

rationales.whyCorrect: The residual volume of 75 mL is below the hold parameter of 100 mL, so the feeding does not need to be held. The nurse should return the residual (to preserve electrolytes), flush the tube, administer the medication, and resume the feeding. Discarding the residual (C) wastes digestive fluids.
rationales.eli10:
- The leftover in the stomach is 75 mL. The limit is 100 mL. It is under the limit, so it is okay.

- Put the leftover back (it has stuff the body needs). Flush the tube with water. Give the medicine. Restart the feeding.

- Only hold if the leftover is over the limit.

- Under limit = safe to continue.

questions.stem: The nurse is helping a client with meal planning after a new diagnosis of hypertension. Which food choice indicates the client needs further teaching?

options.text: Fresh fruit salad with unsalted nuts.
Baked skinless chicken breast with steamed vegetables.
Canned vegetable soup with saltine crackers.
Brown rice with grilled fish and a side salad with olive oil dressing.

rationales.whyCorrect: Canned vegetable soup with saltine crackers is typically very high in sodium, which is contraindicated for a client with hypertension. Fresh fruit and unsalted nuts (A), baked chicken and steamed vegetables (B), and brown rice with grilled fish (D) are all low-sodium, heart-healthy choices.
rationales.eli10:
- Canned soup and saltine crackers are loaded with salt. Salt raises blood pressure.

- The client with high blood pressure needs low-salt foods.

- Fresh foods, grilled meats, and unsalted items are better choices.

- Canned and processed = usually high salt.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client's intravenous (IV) site and notes the following: the site is cool to touch, pale, and swollen, and the client reports pain. The IV solution is no longer infusing. What complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Phlebitis.
Air embolism.
Infiltration.
Infection at the IV site.

rationales.whyCorrect: Infiltration occurs when IV fluid leaks into surrounding tissue. Signs include coolness, pallor, swelling, pain, and a slowed or stopped infusion. Phlebitis (A) presents as warmth, redness, and tenderness along the vein. Air embolism (B) presents with sudden respiratory distress. Infection (D) presents with redness, warmth, and purulence.
rationales.eli10:
- The IV fluid is leaking out of the vein into the tissue.

- The skin looks pale and feels cold and puffy. It hurts. The fluid stopped dripping.

- The nurse must remove the IV and start a new one in a different spot.

- Pale, cold, puffy, painful = IV is out of the vein.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about self-catheterization. Which statement by the client indicates an understanding of the procedure?

options.text: "I should use the same catheter for a week before replacing it."
"I should perform hand hygiene and use clean technique when inserting the catheter."
"I can skip catheterization if I feel like I do not need to empty my bladder."
"I should insert the catheter only halfway to prevent bladder irritation."

rationales.whyCorrect: Self-catheterization should be performed using clean technique (hand hygiene, clean gloves, clean catheter) in the home setting. The catheter should be single-use or cleaned and reused according to specific instructions, not reused for a week without proper cleaning (A). Skipping catheterization (C) can lead to urinary retention and bladder damage.
rationales.eli10:
- Clean technique means wash hands well and use a clean catheter each time.

- Sterile technique is for the hospital. Clean is enough for home.

- Do not reuse a catheter for a week without cleaning it properly.

- Always empty the bladder on schedule, even if you do not feel the need.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing discharge teaching to a client who has a new colostomy. The client asks, "Will I be able to swim or shower with the pouching system on?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You will need to remove the pouch before swimming or showering."
"Yes, the pouching system is waterproof and designed to stay in place during swimming and showering."
"You should avoid swimming entirely because of the risk of infection."
"You can shower but must cover the pouch with plastic wrap and tape."

rationales.whyCorrect: Modern colostomy pouching systems are designed to be waterproof and can remain in place during swimming, showering, and bathing. The client does not need to remove the pouch (A), avoid swimming (C), or use plastic wrap (D).
rationales.eli10:
- The colostomy bag is waterproof. The client can swim, shower, and bathe with it on.

- It sticks to the skin and stays in place in water.

- No need to take it off. No need for plastic wrap.

- Life with a colostomy includes swimming and normal activities.

questions.stem: A client on bed rest has developed a red, warm, and tender area on the right calf. The nurse suspects deep-vein thrombosis (DVT). What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Massage the area to break up the clot.
Keep the client on bed rest, elevate the extremity, and notify the healthcare provider.
Apply a heating pad to the area and encourage the client to walk.
Measure the circumference of both calves and document the difference.

rationales.whyCorrect: If DVT is suspected, the priority is to keep the client on bed rest, elevate the affected extremity to reduce swelling, and notify the healthcare provider. The leg should not be massaged (A) because this could dislodge the clot. A heating pad (C) may be ordered but encouraging ambulation before DVT is ruled out is dangerous. Measuring calf circumference (D) is appropriate documentation but not the priority action.
rationales.eli10:
- The nurse thinks there might be a blood clot in the leg. Keep the client in bed with the leg raised.

- Tell the provider right away. Do not rub the leg. Do not let the client walk.

- Walking or rubbing could knock the clot loose.

- Bed rest, leg up, call the provider.

questions.stem: The home-care nurse is assessing an older adult client who lives alone. Which finding presents the greatest safety concern?

options.text: The client has a clutter-free home with handrails in the bathroom.
The client has several throw rugs on the hardwood floors and keeps the lighting dim.
The client uses a walker and wears well-fitting, non-skid shoes indoors.
The client has a personal emergency response system pendant around the neck.

rationales.whyCorrect: Throw rugs are a major tripping hazard for older adults, and dim lighting makes it difficult to see obstacles, increasing fall risk. Handrails (A), a walker with non-skid shoes (C), and an emergency response pendant (D) are all safety features.
rationales.eli10:
- Throw rugs are easy to trip on. Dim lights make it hard to see.

- Together, they create a very high risk for falling.

- Remove the rugs. Turn up the lights.

- Clear floors and bright lights save older adults from falls.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing passive range-of-motion (ROM) exercises to a client who is immobile. At which point should the nurse stop the movement during each ROM exercise?

options.text: When the client reports mild discomfort.
When the nurse feels resistance in the joint.
When the joint has been moved 180 degrees.
When the client asks the nurse to continue.

rationales.whyCorrect: During passive ROM, the nurse should move the joint only to the point of resistance. Moving beyond resistance can cause injury to muscles, ligaments, or the joint capsule. Mild discomfort (A) may be acceptable; resistance is the stop point. A specific degree (C) varies by joint.
rationales.eli10:
- The nurse moves the client's arm or leg until the joint naturally stops.

- Do not push past where it stops. That could tear something.

- Move to the point of gentle resistance, then stop.

- Do not force. Do not push.

questions.stem: The nurse is administering an enema to a client. The client reports cramping during the administration. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the enema at the current rate and reassure the client.
Stop the enema immediately and remove the rectal tube.
Slow the flow of the enema solution or temporarily clamp the tubing until the cramping subsides.
Increase the flow rate to finish the enema faster and reduce the duration of cramping.

rationales.whyCorrect: Cramping during enema administration is common and is caused by distention of the colon. The nurse should slow the flow rate or temporarily clamp the tubing to allow the cramping to subside, then resume at a slower rate. Continuing at the same rate (A) or increasing (D) worsens cramping. Removing the tube (B) is unnecessary in most cases.
rationales.eli10:
- The enema fluid is stretching the bowel, causing cramps.

- Slow down the flow or pinch the tube to pause. Let the cramp pass.

- Then start again slowly.

- Do not push through the cramp. Pause and let it settle.

questions.stem: A client who has been NPO (nothing by mouth) for 12 hours is now allowed to resume oral intake. Which food or fluid should the nurse offer first?

options.text: A full liquid meal including milk, pudding, and ice cream.
A regular diet tray including solid foods.
Clear liquids such as water or apple juice and advance as tolerated.
Carbonated beverages and spicy foods to stimulate appetite.

rationales.whyCorrect: After being NPO, the client should begin with clear liquids to assess tolerance and the return of peristalsis, then advance the diet as tolerated. Starting with full liquids (A) or a regular diet (B) could cause nausea, vomiting, or aspiration if bowel function has not returned.
rationales.eli10:
- After not eating or drinking for 12 hours, start slow. Give clear liquids (water, apple juice, broth).

- See how the stomach handles it. If okay, move to heavier liquids, then soft food, then regular food.

- Do not start with milk or solid food. Too much too fast can make the client sick.

- Start with see-through liquids.

questions.stem: The nurse is discharging a client who has a prescription for a transdermal medication patch. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: "Apply the new patch over the old patch to ensure continuous medication delivery."
"Remove the old patch, clean the skin, and apply the new patch to a different, clean, and dry area."
"Apply the patch to the same site on the opposite side of the body each time."
"Cut the patch in half if you feel the dose is too strong."

rationales.whyCorrect: When applying a new transdermal patch, the old patch must be removed, the skin cleaned, and the new patch applied to a different dry, clean area to prevent skin irritation and ensure proper absorption. Applying over the old patch (A) prevents new medication from being absorbed. Rotating to the same site (C) can cause skin breakdown. Cutting the patch (D) can alter the medication release rate.
rationales.eli10:
- Take the old patch off. Wash the skin. Put the new patch on a different spot.

- Never put a new patch on top of the old one. The medicine will not get through.

- Rotate spots so the skin does not get irritated.

- Never cut a patch. It changes how much medicine comes out.

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a client's use of an incentive spirometer after abdominal surgery. Which observation indicates that the client is using the device correctly?

options.text: The client exhales forcefully into the device mouthpiece.
The client inhales slowly and deeply through the mouthpiece, holds the breath for 3 seconds, and then exhales.
The client uses the device while lying flat in bed.
The client uses the device once per shift.

rationales.whyCorrect: Correct use of an incentive spirometer involves inhaling slowly and deeply through the mouthpiece to raise the piston or balls, holding the breath for about 3 seconds to maintain alveolar inflation, and then exhaling. Exhaling into the device (A) is incorrect. The client should be sitting upright (C), not lying flat. Use should be every 1 to 2 hours while awake (D), not once per shift.
rationales.eli10:
- Sit up straight. Put the mouthpiece in your mouth.

- Breathe in slowly and deeply — watch the ball rise. Hold the breath for 3 seconds. Then breathe out.

- Do this every 1 to 2 hours while awake.

- Deep breaths keep the lungs open and prevent infection.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has a nasogastric tube connected to low intermittent suction. The client reports a dry mouth and sore throat. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Provide frequent oral care, including mouth rinses, lip moisturizer, and oral swabs.
Remove the NG tube and tell the provider the client is uncomfortable.
Offer the client ice chips to swallow frequently.
Increase the suction pressure to reduce the amount of time the tube must be in place.

rationales.whyCorrect: Frequent oral care (mouth rinses, oral swabs, lip moisturizer) helps relieve the discomfort of dry mouth and sore throat from an NG tube. Removing the tube (B) requires a provider order and would interrupt therapy. Ice chips (C) may not be allowed depending on the reason for the NG tube. Increasing suction (D) does not address the complaint and could damage gastric mucosa.
rationales.eli10:
- The tube in the nose and throat makes the mouth dry and throat sore.

- The nurse provides mouth care often: wet swabs, rinses, and lip balm.

- This helps the client feel more comfortable without removing the tube.

- Mouth care is one of the kindest things a nurse can do.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with urge incontinence about bladder-training techniques. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: "Void as soon as you feel the urge to prevent leakage."
"Gradually increase the time between voiding to help the bladder hold more urine."
"Drink less water during the day to decrease the amount of urine your body makes."
"Perform the Valsalva maneuver (bearing down) when voiding to empty the bladder completely."

rationales.whyCorrect: Bladder training for urge incontinence involves gradually increasing the interval between voiding to help the bladder hold more urine and reduce the frequency of urgency episodes. Voiding as soon as the urge occurs (A) reinforces the urgency cycle. Decreasing fluid intake (C) causes concentrated urine that irritates the bladder. Valsalva (D) is used for stress incontinence, not urge incontinence.
rationales.eli10:
- The client's bladder feels the urge too soon and too often.

- Bladder training slowly teaches the bladder to wait longer. Start by waiting 5 extra minutes, then 10, then more.

- Do not run to the bathroom at the first urge — that trains the bladder to be more urgent.

- Drink normal amounts. Waiting practice helps the bladder stretch and calm down.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to assist a client with a sitz bath. What is the primary purpose of a sitz bath?

options.text: To provide full-body relaxation and stress reduction.
To cleanse and promote comfort and healing in the perineal or anal area.
To reduce a high fever through tepid water immersion.
To exercise the lower extremities in a buoyant environment.

rationales.whyCorrect: A sitz bath involves sitting in warm water that covers only the perineal and anal area. Its primary purpose is to cleanse, promote comfort, reduce inflammation, and promote healing after perineal or rectal surgery or childbirth. It is not for full-body relaxation (A), fever reduction (C), or exercise (D).
rationales.eli10:
- A sitz bath is a small tub you sit in so warm water covers just the bottom area.

- It helps clean and soothe the area after having a baby, rectal surgery, or hemorrhoids.

- It is warm and comforting but only covers the bottom, not the whole body.

- Sitz = sit. Warm water on the perineal area.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who has had diarrhea for 3 days. Which assessment finding is most concerning?

options.text: The client reports abdominal cramping.
The client's skin turgor is tented and mucous membranes are dry.
The client states they have had 5 loose stools today.
The client reports feeling tired and weak.

rationales.whyCorrect: Tented skin turgor and dry mucous membranes indicate significant dehydration from 3 days of diarrhea. This is the most concerning finding because severe dehydration can lead to electrolyte imbalances, hypotension, and shock. Cramping (A), frequency (C), and fatigue (D) are expected with diarrhea and less immediately dangerous than dehydration.
rationales.eli10:
- Three days of diarrhea means the body has lost a lot of water.

- The skin stays pinched up when pulled (tented). The mouth and lips are dry. These are signs of serious dehydration.

- Dehydration can be dangerous. The body needs fluids replaced.

- Cramps, tiredness, and many loose stools are expected. Dry, tented skin is the danger sign.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is being taught about foot care. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?

options.text: "I should soak my feet in hot water every night to soften calluses."
"I should inspect my feet daily and wear well-fitting shoes at all times."
"I can trim my corns and calluses with over-the-counter medicated pads."
"I should go barefoot at home to let my feet breathe."

rationales.whyCorrect: Daily foot inspection and wearing well-fitting shoes at all times are essential for preventing diabetic foot complications (ulcers, infections). Soaking in hot water (A) can cause burns because diabetic neuropathy may prevent the client from feeling excessive heat. Medicated corn pads (C) can cause chemical burns. Going barefoot (D) greatly increases injury risk.
rationales.eli10:
- The client with diabetes must check their feet every day and always wear shoes that fit well.

- Even a tiny cut can become a big infection because diabetes slows healing and reduces feeling.

- Never soak in hot water — you may not feel the burn. Never go barefoot.

- Protect your feet. They are precious.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer an intramuscular injection of an irritating medication. Which technique is most appropriate?

options.text: Use the Z-track method to prevent the medication from leaking into subcutaneous tissue.
Massage the injection site vigorously after administration to disperse the medication.
Administer the injection rapidly to minimize the time the needle is in the muscle.
Inject the medication into the subcutaneous tissue instead of the muscle to reduce pain.

rationales.whyCorrect: The Z-track method displaces the skin and subcutaneous tissue before injection, creating a zigzag path that seals the medication in the muscle and prevents it from leaking back into subcutaneous tissue, which can cause irritation and staining. Vigorous massage (B) can push the medication into subcutaneous tissue. The injection should be administered slowly to allow tissue expansion, not rapidly (C). Subcutaneous injection (D) would not deliver the medication to the muscle.
rationales.eli10:
- Some medicines irritate the skin layer. The Z-track method keeps the medicine in the muscle.

- Pull the skin to the side. Give the shot. Let the skin snap back. This creates a zigzag path that seals the medicine in.

- Do not rub the spot. Rubbing can push the medicine back up.

- Z-track = seal the medicine in the muscle.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who is on bed rest and has been turned to the left lateral position. Which area is at greatest risk for pressure injury in this position?

options.text: The sacrum.
The left trochanter (hip).
The occiput (back of the head).
The heels.

rationales.whyCorrect: In the left lateral position, the left trochanter (hip bone) bears the most pressure from the body's weight pressing against the mattress. The sacrum (A) is at risk in the supine position. The occiput (C) is at risk when the head rests against a surface. The heels (D) are at risk in any position when resting on the mattress.
rationales.eli10:
- When lying on the left side, the left hip bone presses hardest into the bed.

- That is the spot most likely to get a pressure sore.

- Check the hip, ear, shoulder, and ankle on the side that is down.

- Change positions every 2 hours to move the pressure to different spots.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing discharge teaching about a high-fiber diet to a client with chronic constipation. The client asks, "How much water should I drink each day?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Drink only when you feel thirsty."
"Drink at least 8 to 10 glasses (2,000 to 2,500 mL) of water each day unless your provider has restricted your fluids."
"You only need extra water if your urine is dark yellow."
"Avoid water and drink juice instead because juice has more fiber."

rationales.whyCorrect: A high-fiber diet requires adequate fluid intake (at least 2,000 to 2,500 mL/day unless contraindicated) to allow the fiber to absorb water and form soft, bulky stools. Drinking only when thirsty (A) may not provide enough fluid. Dark urine (C) is a late sign of dehydration. Juice (D) does not have more fiber and may have excess sugar.
rationales.eli10:
- Fiber is like a sponge — it soaks up water to make poop soft and easy to pass.

- Without enough water, fiber turns into a dry, hard plug.

- Drink 8 to 10 glasses of water a day, unless the doctor limits your fluids.

- Fiber + water = soft, easy bowel movements. Fiber without water = constipation.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer digoxin to a client. Before administration, the nurse assesses the client's apical pulse and finds it to be 54 beats per minute. The prescription parameters state to hold the medication if the pulse is below 60. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Administer the medication and recheck the pulse in 30 minutes.
Hold the medication, document the pulse, and notify the healthcare provider.
Administer half the prescribed dose and document the adjustment.
Ask the client if they feel well enough to receive the medication.

rationales.whyCorrect: Digoxin slows the heart rate, and an apical pulse below 60 beats per minute (or the prescribed hold parameter) is an indication to hold the medication. The nurse should hold the medication, document the finding, and notify the provider. Administering the medication (A) could cause severe bradycardia. The nurse cannot independently change the dose (C) or base the decision on how the client feels (D).
rationales.eli10:
- Digoxin slows the heart. The heart is already beating slowly at 54.

- If the nurse gives the medicine, the heart could slow down too much — that is dangerous.

- The nurse does not give the medicine, writes it down, and tells the provider.

- Slow heart + digoxin = hold the medicine.

questions.stem: A client is receiving IV heparin. The nurse notes that the client's gums bleed during oral care and there are multiple new bruises on the client's arms. The aPTT result is 110 seconds (therapeutic range: 60–80 seconds). What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Document the findings and continue the heparin at the current rate.
Stop the heparin infusion and notify the healthcare provider immediately.
Increase the heparin rate to prevent clot formation.
Administer vitamin K IM as an antidote.

rationales.whyCorrect: Bleeding gums, new bruising, and an aPTT of 110 seconds (well above therapeutic range) indicate excessive anticoagulation and risk of serious bleeding. The heparin infusion must be stopped immediately, and the provider notified. Continuing (A) or increasing (C) the rate would worsen the bleeding. Vitamin K (D) is the antidote for warfarin, not heparin (protamine sulfate is the heparin antidote).
rationales.eli10:
- The client's blood is way too thin. Gums are bleeding, bruises are forming, and the lab test shows the blood is dangerously thin.

- The nurse stops the heparin drip right now and calls the provider.

- The antidote for heparin is protamine sulfate, not vitamin K.

- Too thin blood = stop the thinner.

questions.stem: The healthcare provider orders: "Cefazolin 1 g IV every 8 hours." The pharmacy supplies cefazolin 1 g in 50 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride to be infused over 30 minutes. The IV tubing has a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the correct drip rate in drops per minute (gtt/min)?

options.text: 15 gtt/min.
25 gtt/min.
50 gtt/min.
75 gtt/min.

rationales.whyCorrect: Drip rate calculation: Volume (50 mL) × drop factor (15 gtt/mL) ÷ time (30 min) = 750 ÷ 30 = 25 gtt/min. The formula is: gtt/min = (volume in mL × drop factor in gtt/mL) ÷ time in minutes.
rationales.eli10:
- The math: 50 mL × 15 drops per mL = 750 total drops. Divide by 30 minutes = 25 drops per minute.

- Count the drops with a watch. Make sure it drips at 25 drops every minute.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has been prescribed warfarin. Which statement by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I should use an electric razor instead of a blade to shave."
"I can take over-the-counter ibuprofen for headaches."
"I do not need to have my blood checked while taking this medication."
"I should eat more green leafy vegetables to help this medication work better."

rationales.whyCorrect: Warfarin increases bleeding risk, so the client should use an electric razor instead of a blade to prevent cuts. Ibuprofen (B) can increase bleeding risk and should be avoided unless approved by the provider. Regular blood monitoring (INR) (C) is essential. Green leafy vegetables (D) are high in vitamin K (the antidote to warfarin) and should be eaten in consistent amounts, not increased.
rationales.eli10:
- Warfarin makes blood thinner. A blade razor could cause a bad cut that bleeds a lot.

- Use an electric razor to stay safe.

- Do not take ibuprofen — it also thins the blood.

- Keep eating the same amount of greens. Too much green leafy food can stop the medicine from working.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer an IV antibiotic via a peripheral line. The nurse checks the IV site and notes that the area is red, warm, and tender along the vein. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and apply a warm compress.
Administer the medication because the IV is still functional.
Stop the infusion, remove the IV catheter, and restart the IV at a different site.
Flush the IV catheter with normal saline and, if it flushes easily, administer the medication.

rationales.whyCorrect: Redness, warmth, and tenderness along the vein are signs of phlebitis (inflammation of the vein). The IV should be discontinued and restarted at a different site. Continuing the infusion (A, B) could worsen the phlebitis. Flushing (D) does not address the inflammation and could cause further damage.
rationales.eli10:
- The vein is red, warm, and sore. This is called phlebitis — the vein is irritated and inflamed.

- Take the IV out. Put a new one in a different spot.

- Do not keep using an angry vein. It will only get worse.

- Red, warm, sore vein = remove the IV.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed "furosemide 40 mg PO daily." Before administering the medication, which assessment is most important?

options.text: Assessing the client's bowel sounds.
Checking the client's blood pressure and serum potassium level.
Measuring the client's abdominal girth.
Checking the client's pupil reaction.

rationales.whyCorrect: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that lowers blood pressure and can cause hypokalemia (low potassium). The nurse must assess blood pressure before administration (to avoid hypotension) and check the potassium level because hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity and cardiac dysrhythmias. Bowel sounds (A), abdominal girth (C), and pupils (D) are not priority assessments for this medication.
rationales.eli10:
- Furosemide makes the body pee out extra water and salt. It can lower blood pressure and potassium levels.

- Check blood pressure first. If it is already low, the medicine could make it dangerously low.

- Check potassium too. Low potassium can cause heart problems.

- Blood pressure and potassium matter most with this medicine.

questions.stem: The nurse is administering an intramuscular injection using the Z-track method. Which action is correct?

options.text: Insert the needle at a 45-degree angle.
Massage the site vigorously for 30 seconds after injection.
Pull the skin laterally before inserting the needle, and release the skin after withdrawing the needle.
Inject the medication rapidly using a 1-mL syringe.

rationales.whyCorrect: The Z-track method involves pulling the skin laterally (to the side) before needle insertion, administering the medication, waiting 10 seconds, then withdrawing the needle and releasing the skin. This creates a zigzag path that seals the medication in the muscle. IM injections use a 90-degree angle, not 45 degrees (A) (that is for subcutaneous). Massage (B) is contraindicated with Z-track. The injection should not be rapid (D).
rationales.eli10:
- Pull the skin to the side. Give the shot. Wait 10 seconds. Pull the needle out. Let the skin snap back.

- This makes a zigzag path that keeps the medicine deep in the muscle where it belongs.

- Do not rub the spot. Rubbing pushes medicine back up.

- 90-degree angle, not 45.

questions.stem: The nurse is calculating an IV flow rate. The order reads: "1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride to infuse over 8 hours." The IV tubing has a drop factor of 20 gtt/mL. What is the correct flow rate in gtt/min? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

options.text: 21 gtt/min.
32 gtt/min.
42 gtt/min.
52 gtt/min.

rationales.whyCorrect: Flow rate calculation: 1,000 mL × 20 gtt/mL = 20,000 gtt. Divided by 480 minutes (8 hours × 60 min/hr) = 41.67 gtt/min. Rounded to the nearest whole number = 42 gtt/min.
rationales.eli10:
- The math: 1,000 mL × 20 drops per mL = 20,000 drops.

- 8 hours = 480 minutes.

- 20,000 ÷ 480 = about 42 drops per minute.

- Set the drip to 42 drops every minute.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has a blood glucose level of 52 mg/dL and is awake but shaky and diaphoretic. What should the nurse administer first?

options.text: Insulin lispro subcutaneously per sliding-scale order.
15 grams of a rapid-acting carbohydrate, such as 4 ounces of orange juice.
A complex-carbohydrate snack, such as a peanut butter sandwich.
Glucagon intramuscularly as ordered.

rationales.whyCorrect: A blood glucose of 52 mg/dL indicates hypoglycemia. The client is awake and can swallow safely. The nurse should administer 15 grams of a rapid-acting carbohydrate (such as 4 ounces of juice or glucose tablets) and recheck blood glucose in 15 minutes ("Rule of 15"). Insulin (A) would lower the glucose further. A complex snack (C) is given after the glucose normalizes. Glucagon (D) is for unconscious clients.
rationales.eli10:
- Blood sugar is too low (52). The client is awake and can drink.

- Give fast sugar: 4 ounces of orange juice or 3 glucose tablets.

- Check blood sugar again in 15 minutes. If still low, give more.

- Do not give insulin — that lowers sugar. Do not give glucagon — that is for when the client is unconscious.

- The rule: 15 grams of fast sugar, wait 15 minutes, check again.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a client's medication list and notes that the client is taking both lisinopril and spironolactone. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?

options.text: Serum sodium level.
Serum potassium level.
Serum calcium level.
Serum magnesium level.

rationales.whyCorrect: Lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) and spironolactone (a potassium-sparing diuretic) both increase serum potassium levels. Concurrent use increases the risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia. The nurse must monitor the serum potassium level closely. Sodium (A), calcium (C), and magnesium (D) are less directly affected by this combination.
rationales.eli10:
- Both medicines raise potassium in the blood. Taking them together can make potassium go too high.

- High potassium can stop the heart. The nurse must check the potassium level closely.

- Do not let potassium get too high. It is a silent danger.

questions.stem: A client who is receiving a blood transfusion reports feeling itchy and the nurse notes hives on the client's chest. Vital signs remain stable. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Continue the transfusion and administer diphenhydramine as prescribed.
Stop the transfusion immediately and disconnect the blood tubing.
Slow the transfusion rate and notify the healthcare provider.
Pause the transfusion, maintain IV access with normal saline, and notify the healthcare provider.

rationales.whyCorrect: Itching and hives with stable vital signs suggest a mild allergic transfusion reaction. The nurse should pause the transfusion, maintain IV access with normal saline (to keep the vein open for emergency medications if needed), and notify the provider. Stopping and disconnecting (B) is for severe reactions. Continuing (A) or just slowing (C) could allow the reaction to worsen.
rationales.eli10:
- The client has hives and itching from the blood. This is a mild allergic reaction.

- Stop the blood. Keep the IV open with salt water. Call the provider.

- Do not keep giving blood. Do not take the IV out.

- The provider may order Benadryl and then allow the blood to continue.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer insulin glargine and insulin lispro to a client. Which action is correct?

options.text: Mix the two insulins in the same syringe before administration.
Draw up the insulin glargine first, then the insulin lispro.
Administer the two insulins as separate injections.
Administer insulin lispro first, wait 30 minutes, then administer insulin glargine.

rationales.whyCorrect: Insulin glargine (long-acting) should NEVER be mixed with other insulins because mixing alters its pH and absorption characteristics. It must be administered as a separate injection. Only short-acting (regular) and intermediate-acting (NPH) insulins can be mixed. Waiting 30 minutes (D) is unnecessary.
rationales.eli10:
- Glargine is a long-acting insulin. It cannot be mixed with any other insulin in the same syringe.

- Give glargine as its own shot. Give lispro as a separate shot.

- Only regular (clear) and NPH (cloudy) can be mixed.

- Two insulins = two separate shots if one is glargine.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about taking ferrous sulfate (iron) for iron-deficiency anemia. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: "Take this medication with milk to improve absorption."
"Take this medication on an empty stomach with water or juice containing vitamin C."
"Expect your stools to turn black and tarry; this is a sign of bleeding and should be reported immediately."
"Take this medication at bedtime to avoid stomach discomfort."

rationales.whyCorrect: Iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach with water or juice containing vitamin C (which enhances absorption). Milk (A) and antacids decrease iron absorption. Iron does cause dark stools (C), but this is an expected effect, not a sign of bleeding. Taking at bedtime (D) may cause GI upset; it is usually taken during the day with vitamin C-containing juice.
rationales.eli10:
- Take iron on an empty stomach. Orange juice helps the body use the iron better.

- Iron makes poop dark — that is normal, not blood.

- Milk makes iron harder to absorb. Do not take iron with milk.

- Empty stomach + vitamin C juice = best absorption.

questions.stem: A client receiving IV morphine via a patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump is found to have a respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute and is difficult to arouse. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Decrease the PCA pump settings and monitor the client closely.
Stop the PCA infusion, administer naloxone as prescribed, and notify the provider.
Increase the IV fluid rate to flush the morphine from the system.
Encourage the client to take deep breaths and stay awake.

rationales.whyCorrect: A respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute with difficulty arousing indicates opioid-induced respiratory depression — a life-threatening emergency. The nurse must stop the PCA infusion, administer the opioid antagonist naloxone as prescribed, and notify the provider. Decreasing the PCA (A) does not reverse the respiratory depression. IV fluids (C) do not reverse the opioid effect. Encouraging deep breaths (D) is insufficient.
rationales.eli10:
- The morphine is making the client breathe way too slowly (only 8 breaths per minute). They are hard to wake up.

- This is a morphine overdose. Stop the morphine pump.

- Give naloxone (Narcan) — this medicine reverses morphine and helps the client breathe again.

- Call the provider right away. This is an emergency.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer an IV medication through a client's peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line. Before administration, which action is most important?

options.text: Assess the insertion site for signs of infection.
Verify placement by checking for blood return and flushing with normal saline.
Measure the external catheter length and compare it to the insertion length documented.
Ask the client when the PICC line was last used.

rationales.whyCorrect: Before using a PICC line, the nurse must verify patency by checking for blood return and flushing with normal saline without resistance. Assessing the site (A) is important but verifying function is the immediate pre-administration priority. Measuring external length (C) is part of ongoing assessment but not the most important pre-use check. The nurse should verify placement, not rely on the client's report (D).
rationales.eli10:
- Before putting medicine through a PICC line, the nurse pulls back on the syringe to see blood return. Then flushes with salt water to make sure it flows easily.

- This checks that the line is still in the right place and not blocked.

- A clean site is important, but first make sure the line works.

- Blood return + easy flush = safe to use.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has been prescribed metformin for type 2 diabetes. Which statement by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I should stop taking metformin 48 hours before any procedure that uses contrast dye."
"I can drink alcohol freely while taking this medication."
"Metformin can cause my blood sugar to drop too low, so I should always carry a snack."
"I only need to take this medication on days when I eat large meals."

rationales.whyCorrect: Metformin should be held 48 hours before and after procedures using contrast dye due to the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy, which can lead to metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis. Alcohol (B) should be avoided or limited because it increases the risk of lactic acidosis. Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia (C). It must be taken consistently, not only on days with large meals (D).
rationales.eli10:
- If the client needs a test with dye (contrast), stop metformin 2 days before and 2 days after.

- The dye can hurt the kidneys, and metformin can build up to dangerous levels.

- Metformin is an every-day medicine, not just on big meal days.

- Alcohol and metformin do not mix well.

questions.stem: A client is receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central line. The nurse notes that the current TPN bag is nearly empty and the next bag is not yet available from the pharmacy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the TPN at the current rate until the new bag arrives.
Administer 10% dextrose in water at the same rate until the new TPN arrives.
Stop the TPN and clamp the central line.
Administer 0.9% sodium chloride at the same rate until the new TPN arrives.

rationales.whyCorrect: When TPN is temporarily unavailable, a 10% dextrose solution should be administered at the same rate to prevent rebound hypoglycemia from the sudden withdrawal of the high-glucose TPN. Running the bag dry (A) would stop the glucose infusion. Stopping entirely (C) would cause hypoglycemia. Normal saline (D) has no glucose and would not prevent hypoglycemia.
rationales.eli10:
- TPN is high-sugar nutrition. Stopping it suddenly can crash the blood sugar.

- If the next bag is not ready, hang sugar water (10% dextrose) at the same speed.

- This keeps the blood sugar steady until the TPN arrives.

- Never let TPN run dry without a backup sugar solution.

questions.stem: The nurse is administering eye drops to a client. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Place the drop directly onto the center of the cornea.
Pull the lower eyelid down to create a pocket and instill the drop into the conjunctival sac.
Administer the drop into the inner canthus of the eye near the tear duct.
Hold the dropper 6 inches above the eye and allow the drop to fall onto the surface.

rationales.whyCorrect: To administer eye drops correctly, the nurse should pull the lower eyelid down to create a conjunctival sac (pocket) and instill the drop into the sac — not directly onto the cornea (A), which can cause discomfort and blinking. The inner canthus (C) is for punctal occlusion, not drop placement. The dropper should be held about 1 to 2 inches from the eye (D), not 6 inches.
rationales.eli10:
- Gently pull down the lower lid to make a little pocket.

- Drop the medicine into the pocket, not onto the eye itself.

- The dropper should not touch the eye. Hold it about an inch away.

- Drop in the pocket, blink gently, do not rub.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client who develops sudden chest pain, dyspnea, and hypotension 30 minutes after an IV antibiotic infusion was started. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Slow the infusion and monitor the client's vital signs.
Stop the infusion, maintain IV access, administer oxygen, and prepare for emergency interventions.
Notify the pharmacy that the client had a mild reaction to the antibiotic.
Ask the client whether they have ever had this medication before.

rationales.whyCorrect: Sudden chest pain, dyspnea, and hypotension after starting an IV antibiotic strongly suggest an anaphylactic reaction. The priority is to stop the infusion, maintain IV access, administer oxygen, and prepare for emergency interventions (which may include epinephrine, antihistamines, and corticosteroids). Slowing the infusion (A) delays critical treatment. Notifying pharmacy (C) is secondary. Asking history (D) wastes time during an emergency.
rationales.eli10:
- The client is having a severe allergic reaction: chest pain, trouble breathing, blood pressure falling.

- Stop the medicine now. Keep the IV in. Give oxygen. Get ready to give emergency drugs.

- This is anaphylaxis — life-threatening allergy. Act fast.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer enoxaparin subcutaneously. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Aspirate before injecting the medication.
Massage the site for 10 seconds after the injection.
Inject the medication into the abdominal area using a 45- to 90-degree angle without aspirating.
Administer the injection into the deltoid muscle.

rationales.whyCorrect: Enoxaparin (a low-molecular-weight heparin) is administered subcutaneously in the abdomen at a 45- to 90-degree angle. Aspiration (A) is not recommended because it can cause hematoma formation. Massaging the site (B) can also cause bruising and hematoma. The deltoid (D) is not the recommended site for enoxaparin.
rationales.eli10:
- Given as a shot in the belly fat, at least 2 inches from the belly button.

- Do not pull back on the plunger (aspirate). Do not rub the spot.

- Both can cause bruising.

- Pinch the skin, give the shot, let go, do not rub.

questions.stem: A client is receiving IV potassium chloride for a potassium level of 2.9 mEq/L. The nurse notes that the IV site is red, tender, and the client reports burning. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the potassium infusion and apply a warm compress.
Stop the infusion immediately and discontinue the IV.
Flush the IV with normal saline to dilute the potassium.
Increase the infusion rate to complete the dose faster.

rationales.whyCorrect: Potassium is a vesicant and can cause tissue damage if it infiltrates. A red, tender IV site with burning indicates possible infiltration. The infusion must be stopped immediately and the IV discontinued. Slowing the rate (A) still delivers the potassium to the tissue. Flushing (C) would push more potassium into the tissue.
rationales.eli10:
- Potassium leaking out of the vein burns the tissue.

- The IV site is red, sore, and burning. Stop it now. Take the IV out.

- Never keep running potassium when the site hurts.
